title: Eli: Getting Back to School
clinicalAuthorship: AI-assisted synthetic draft; r1 reviewed and authorized for learner publication by the requesting author on 2026-09-27; r2 revision reviewed and authorized by the requesting author on 2026-10-04 (PR #972).
setting: Emergency assessment, inpatient psychiatry, and early-psychosis outpatient care
disclaimer: Entirely fictional; no real patient record was used. For supervised educational discussion only. This is not a treatment protocol or an assessment of learner competence. Medication, disposition, confidentiality, and escalation decisions require the supervising team and applicable local policy.
audience: Shared MS3 and resident learner core; scope follows the learner’s actual supervision arrangements.
timeFrame: Six chapters over approximately three months; chapter numbers are not rotation weeks or a prescribed treatment schedule.

patient.description: Eli is a fictional 22-year-old community-college student who works in a bicycle shop. He wants to finish his certificate and keep his friendships. His sister brings him for help after growing fear, disrupted sleep, and difficulty attending class.
patient.frame: Track the relationship among psychotic symptoms, mood, substance exposure, medication effects, and function without settling the diagnosis too early. Returning to a meaningful life remains a treatment target throughout.

learningObjectives: Describe a psychotic syndrome and update a differential using the timeline, collateral, examination, and observed course.
Explore cannabis use without treating a toxicology result as a causal diagnosis.
Recognize new restlessness as a possible medication adverse effect and request timely reassessment.
Connect shared treatment decisions and physical-health monitoring to the patient's goals.
Complete a handoff with confirmed ownership and respond to early deterioration after discharge.

sources.title: NICE CG178 — Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults

weeks.label: Arrival · day 0
weeks.title: Start with the experience, not the label
weeks.patientState: Eli says classmates have been embedding messages about him in group chats. He sometimes hears a voice commenting on what he is doing when nobody is nearby. He has missed classes for two weeks and slept only a few hours on several nights, but says he feels exhausted rather than unusually energetic. He is guarded, watches the doorway, and can sustain a conversation. He reports using a high-potency cannabis vape most evenings. His sister says, 'He has never been like this.' Eli asks whether telling the truth will automatically mean he cannot leave. No complete safety or medical assessment has yet occurred.
weeks.learnerTask: With the supervising clinician, clarify onset, conviction, distress, thought organization, mood symptoms, substance and medication exposure, and functional change. Ask directly about self-harm, harm to others, command content, and ability to meet basic needs. Review vital signs and the medical assessment. Explain your role and confidentiality limits; do not promise a disposition before assessment.

checklist.prompt: Acknowledge distress while keeping the explanation open.
checklist.example: That sounds frightening, and I don't know yet what is going on with the group chats. I want to understand what you have been noticing and how it is affecting you. Have the voices told you to do anything?

weeks.handoff: Eli describes suspicious beliefs and auditory experiences with disrupted sleep and function. The cause and duration remain uncertain. Cannabis exposure is relevant, but mood, medical, and other psychiatric explanations still need assessment. Report the actual safety findings and missing information to the supervisor before discussing disposition.
weeks.reflectionPrompt: Which observation supports a psychotic syndrome, and which detail would change the immediate response?
weeks.residentExtension: Contrast reduced need for sleep with insomnia and exhaustion. What findings would prompt a broader urgent medical or neurologic evaluation?
weeks.commonMisstep: Equating a psychotic symptom with dangerousness, or arguing about the belief before understanding distress and behavior.

weeks.label: Inpatient · day 2
weeks.title: Collateral changes the timeline
weeks.patientState: After assessment, Eli has agreed to inpatient care. With permission to speak to his sister, the team learns that withdrawal from friends and unusual suspicions began about two months ago; the switch to a stronger cannabis product happened three weeks ago. Eli recalls a few earlier voice-like experiences but cannot date them reliably. Urine testing detects cannabinoids. The initial examination and selected investigations have not identified an acute medical cause, although that does not exclude every cause. No sustained period of elevated mood or increased goal-directed activity has emerged from the history. Eli asks, 'Does the positive test explain all of this?'
weeks.learnerTask: Build one timeline that separates Eli's account, his sister's observations, and verified records. Compare primary psychosis, a substance-related syndrome, and a mood disorder with psychosis; retain medical alternatives when indicated. Identify what future observation would strengthen or weaken each explanation. Discuss the effects and purpose of cannabis use without confrontation.

checklist.prompt: Describe what the new evidence changes and what it cannot establish.
checklist.example: The test tells us cannabis exposure occurred; it does not tell us that cannabis explains every symptom. Your sister noticed changes before the stronger product. We will keep following the timeline with you while treating the distress you are experiencing now.

weeks.handoff: Collateral moves functional decline and some unusual experiences earlier than the recent increase in cannabis potency. A primary psychotic disorder remains a working possibility; a substance contribution remains important. Record the source of each date and the unresolved exposure history. The initial medical evaluation has not established an alternative cause.
weeks.reflectionPrompt: What would you need to learn before replacing a working formulation with a more specific diagnosis?
weeks.residentExtension: Which duration, mood-course, and exposure details are still missing for a specific DSM diagnosis? How would you communicate uncertainty without implying that treatment must wait?
weeks.commonMisstep: Calling a positive cannabinoid result proof of causation, or claiming that a reassuring initial workup excludes all medical causes.

weeks.label: Inpatient · day 5
weeks.title: When apparent agitation may be an adverse effect
weeks.patientState: The supervising prescriber started oral risperidone after discussing options and obtaining baseline assessments. Eli now sleeps longer and is less preoccupied with the messages. Since the dose was increased two days ago, however, he paces, repeatedly stands during interview, and describes an unbearable internal need to move. He says, 'The voices are quieter, but my body will not let me sit.' Nursing asks whether his illness is getting worse. There is no reported fever or rigidity; a fresh vital-sign review and examination are still needed. Eli is considering refusing the next dose.
weeks.learnerTask: Bring the new distress promptly to the supervisor. Establish its timing against medication changes and ask about subjective restlessness, sleep, anxiety, substance withdrawal, and safety. Review movement findings, vital signs, and other adverse effects. Discuss whether akathisia fits; the prescriber determines any regimen change. Do not translate pacing alone into a request for more antipsychotic medication.

checklist.prompt: Treat the reported adverse effect as meaningful clinical information.
checklist.example: You are telling me that the voices have eased while a new kind of restlessness has become very difficult. I will bring that to the prescriber now so we can assess whether the treatment is contributing. We should discuss it before assuming the original symptoms are worsening.

weeks.handoff: Psychotic distress has lessened, but new subjective and observable restlessness followed a medication adjustment. Possible akathisia needs prompt review alongside other explanations. Report safety findings, vital signs, movement examination, and medication timing. Ask the prescriber to state the reassessment plan and when response will be checked.
weeks.reflectionPrompt: What changed because you asked how the pacing feels instead of only observing that it occurs?
weeks.residentExtension: How would fever, rigidity, autonomic change, altered consciousness, or severe suicidal distress change the urgency and differential?
weeks.commonMisstep: Increasing treatment on the assumption that all motor restlessness is worsening psychosis.

weeks.label: Transition · day 10
weeks.title: A referral is not yet a connection
weeks.patientState: After prescriber reassessment and a revised regimen, Eli reports less restlessness. He still occasionally hears the commentary but feels less frightened and participates in discharge planning. He wants help returning to class. His sister offers support, but Eli agrees only to sharing the practical plan and early warning signs. An early-psychosis referral has been sent; intake is not yet confirmed. His family assumes the first visit is already booked, and the proposed medication pickup has not been verified.
weeks.learnerTask: Present a transition plan for supervisor review that includes current safety findings, Eli's goals, medication access, tolerability, and physical-health monitoring. Confirm who will contact the receiving service and who retains responsibility until it accepts the handoff. Clarify permission for family involvement. Include support for education and substance-use goals, not just medication follow-up.

checklist.prompt: Make an incomplete transition visible without blaming the patient.
checklist.example: Getting back to class matters to you. We have sent the referral, but we do not yet have a confirmed visit. Before the plan is finalized, we need to verify the appointment, medication pickup, and which team you can reach while you are waiting.

weeks.handoff: Eli's distress and restlessness have improved, with residual symptoms. Early-psychosis intake and medication access are unconfirmed. The team needs to name the clinician responsible for bridging care and verify the receiving clinician's acceptance under the local process. Bring unresolved items to today's review and document the expected callback and fallback if contact fails.
weeks.reflectionPrompt: Which part of this discharge plan exists only on paper?
weeks.residentExtension: Build a monitoring handoff that specifies who reviews metabolic and movement findings and who responds to adverse effects between visits.
weeks.commonMisstep: Treating a sent referral as an accepted transfer of care or treating family involvement as unlimited permission to disclose.

weeks.label: Outpatient · week 6
weeks.title: Reopen the plan when life intervenes
weeks.patientState: Eli attended the confirmed intake and has begun supported education work. This week he misses a visit. A phone conversation reveals that he has skipped several risperidone doses because of increased appetite and worries about weight. He has resumed cannabis use with friends and slept less over the last three nights. The group-chat messages feel significant again. He denies a current intention to harm himself or others but says he is becoming frightened. His sister has noticed changes, but the team has not yet heard her account.
weeks.learnerTask: Within the service's supervision and outreach process, report the evolving symptoms promptly and help arrange clinician reassessment. Revisit safety, sleep, functioning, medication effects and access, and the meaning of cannabis use. Ask permission for collateral. Help the team agree on the urgency of contact and an escalation plan rather than waiting for the next routine appointment.

checklist.prompt: Invite the reason for missed treatment and connect it to an actionable review.
checklist.example: The appetite change and worry about weight deserve attention. I also hear that sleep and the messages are changing again. Let's bring both concerns to your clinician today so we can work out what support and treatment changes may help.

weeks.handoff: After initial outpatient engagement, missed doses, resumed cannabis use, and shorter sleep accompany renewed suspiciousness. These associations do not establish a single cause. Relay current safety findings and arrange a timely clinician review; document the receiving person and response, including what to do if Eli cannot be reached.
weeks.reflectionPrompt: How does the plan change when skipped medication is understood as information about tolerability?
weeks.residentExtension: If Eli asks about an injectable option, what preference, tolerability, access, and continuity questions should precede a prescribing decision?
weeks.commonMisstep: Using 'noncompliant' as the formulation, or interpreting denial of current intent as completion of a safety assessment.

weeks.label: Outpatient · month 3
weeks.title: Describe recovery in the patient's terms
weeks.patientState: Following clinician reassessment, Eli and the team revised his medication and support plan. He is attending one class and a weekly therapy visit. Appetite concerns remain part of follow-up, and physical-health monitoring has an assigned clinician. He has reduced cannabis use and is considering a period without it. He occasionally hears the commentary during stress and knows how to report a change. Eli says, 'I am doing better, but I do not want every conversation to be about my illness.' The precise long-term diagnosis remains under review.
weeks.learnerTask: Give a longitudinal formulation that connects initial symptoms, collateral, substance exposure, treatment effects, and the response to the setback. Identify current goals, residual concerns, and unanswered diagnostic questions. Summarize the shared early-warning plan and monitoring ownership. Ask what Eli wants the next clinician to understand about his life beyond symptoms.

checklist.prompt: Center function and preferences alongside symptoms.
checklist.example: You are back in a class and making room for friendships again. Those changes matter alongside the symptoms. What would you like the next stage of care to help you do, and what should we keep watching together?

weeks.handoff: Eli's course includes psychosis, uncertain substance contribution, medication-associated restlessness, and a setback after discharge. Current gains include study, engagement, and a usable contact plan; residual experiences and tolerability concerns remain. The early-psychosis team owns follow-up and monitoring. Diagnostic specificity will depend on the continuing course.
weeks.reflectionPrompt: What does this trajectory reveal that a single discharge summary could not?
weeks.residentExtension: Give a formulation in which you state what is observed, what is inferred, and which observation would change your leading diagnosis.
weeks.commonMisstep: Defining success only as absent hallucinations or presenting three months of observation as a settled lifetime prognosis.
